articles.summary: Danish bunker supplier and shipowner Monjasa has acquired five sister product tankers from Germany’s Bernhard Schulte in its largest-ever fleet deal, strengthening its marine fuels operations in West Africa. articles.body: Europe Tankers Monjasa seals biggest-ever fleet deal with five-tanker swoop Adis Ajdin November 11, 2026 0 19 1 minute read Monjasa Monjasa Danish bunker supplier and shipowner Monjasa has acquired five sister product tankers from Germany’s Bernhard Schulte in its largest-ever fleet deal, strengthening its marine fuels operations in West Africa. The Fredericia-based group has picked up five 2010- and 2011-built tankers of around 16,500 dwt each. The purchase price has not been disclosed. Four vessels, renamed Monjasa Tracer, Monjasa Tuner, Monjasa Twister and Monjasa Tracker , have already joined the fleet and are trading in West Africa and Northwest Europe. The fifth, Monjasa Trigger , is set to follow by the end of November. The ships previously traded as Eva Schulte, Erika Schulte, Everhard Schulte, Edzard Schulte and Elisabeth Schulte , respectively. The acquisition takes Monjasa’s owned fleet to 20 tankers, alongside around 10 ships on time charter. Group chief executive Anders Østergaard described the purchase as the company’s largest single tonnage acquisition, highlighting the benefits of taking on five identical vessels with established operating costs and technical requirements. “Finding five sister vessels of this quality, at competitive market terms and with an operating profile that fits our existing fleet, is not something you come across every day,” he said. The tankers will initially support Monjasa’s West African operations, although the company also sees opportunities to employ them in commercial freight trading and elsewhere in its global supply network. The deal builds on Monjasa’s earlier tanker investments in West Africa, including the 2023 acquisition of the 68,589 dwt Monjasa Leader and the 13,051 dwt Monjasa Refiner , which were brought in for floating storage and bunker supply operations, respectively. articles.body: The service expansion began with the inaugural call of the 1,781 TEU containership HAIAN ALFA at Dakshin Bharat Gateway Terminal (DBGT) on 7 November 2026. The new call provides southern Indian importers and exporters with additional container shipping connections to Vietnam and other Asian markets. According to the V.O. Chidambaranar Port Authority , the service operates fortnightly, linking Tuticorin with Chennai, Ho Chi Minh City, Hai Phong, Qinzhou and Port Klang. New service strengthens Asian connectivity The expanded CVI service offers scheduled transit times of approximately seven days from Tuticorin to Ho Chi Minh City and ten days to Hai Phong. These connections provide businesses in southern India with additional options for transporting cargo to Vietnamese markets. During its first call at DBGT, HAIAN ALFA handled 823 TEU. The total included 723 TEU of imports, primarily associated with Vietnamese automaker VinFast. The vessel also handled 100 TEU of transshipment cargo destined for Colombo. The terminal operator confirmed the maiden call and highlighted the additional connectivity provided by the expanded service. The Vietnamese-flagged HAIAN ALFA measures 171.9 metres in length and 28.4 metres in beam. The new Tuticorin call expands Hai An’s regional shipping network and provides another connection between India’s southern manufacturing markets and key ports in Southeast Asia. It also strengthens DBGT’s role in supporting international container services at V.O. Chidambaranar Port.

articles.summary: Aberdeen-based well engineering specialist Elemental Energies has secured a two-year contract from Harbour Energy to support the expansion of the Viking carbon capture and storage (CCS) project in the UK southern North Sea. articles.body: Europe Offshore Elemental Energies wins offshore CCS deal from Harbour Energy Bojan Lepic November 11, 2026 0 9 1 minute read Viking CCS Viking CCS Aberdeen-based well engineering specialist Elemental Energies has secured a two-year contract from Harbour Energy to support the expansion of the Viking carbon capture and storage (CCS) project in the UK southern North Sea. The contract covers integrated subsurface, geomechanics and well engineering studies for the Viking East and Viking West storage sites. The work will assess storage capacity, geological containment and carbon dioxide injectivity, helping reduce technical risks associated with the project’s planned expansion. Harbour Energy is developing Viking CCS and holds a 60% operating interest, alongside BP with 40%. The project aims to transport and permanently store carbon dioxide captured from industrial facilities in the Humber region. Its initial phase is designed to store up to 4m tonnes of CO₂ annually from the early 2030s, with Harbour targeting capacity of up to 15m tonnes per year by 2035. The development plans to reuse existing southern North Sea infrastructure, including an offshore pipeline linking the former Theddlethorpe gas terminal to depleted Viking gas reservoirs approximately 2.7 km beneath the seabed. Viking completed front-end engineering design in 2025 and secured development consent for its onshore pipeline the same year. The project received approval for £65.5m ($87.3m) in UK government development funding in July 2026, with that support retained in the latest government budget. A final investment decision remains outstanding, with the latest engineering award intended to support further development of the project’s offshore storage capacity. articles.title: Freightos launches AI-powered platform for freight forwarders
articles.summary: Freightos has launched a new generation of its Freightos for Forwarders platform, bringing artificial intelligence into freight quoting, booking and rate management. The upgraded platform supports both air and ocean freight operations. It combines carrier rates, market intelligence and digital booking tools in a...
articles.body: Freightos has launched a new generation of its Freightos for Forwarders platform, bringing artificial intelligence into freight quoting, booking and rate management. The upgraded platform supports both air and ocean freight operations. It combines carrier rates, market intelligence and digital booking tools in a single system. According to Freightos, the new version aims to reduce manual work and help forwarders respond to customer enquiries more quickly. The platform is now available globally to international air and ocean freight forwarders. AI tools simplify freight quoting and booking A key feature of the upgraded platform is the introduction of AI agents into everyday freight forwarding workflows. These tools process customer enquiries from different communication channels. They can also apply customer-specific procedures, pricing rules and profit margins to prepare freight quotations. Freightos says the system can generate ready-to-send quotes in seconds. This allows forwarding teams to spend less time transferring information between emails, spreadsheets and booking systems. The platform also brings together contract rates, promotional tariffs and surcharges. As a result, users can manage pricing information alongside live carrier capacity and booking options. In addition, Freightos Terminal benchmarks provide market data to help forwarders assess the competitiveness of their rates. Pablo Pinillos, Chief Executive Officer of Freightos, said the company has developed the new platform around its existing carrier connectivity and operational data. “AI is only as powerful as the data, connectivity, and workflows behind it,” said Pinillos. He added that the company’s goal is to reduce administrative work while helping freight forwarders focus on customer service and business growth. Freightos expands connectivity and system integration The new platform connects forwarders with more than 75 global air and ocean carriers through Freightos’ existing network. It also provides access to the 7LFreight trucking network, allowing users to manage additional transportation options alongside their international freight operations. Forwarders can maintain their own rates, customer agreements and commercial rules within the system. They can then use these settings when preparing quotations and managing bookings. Meanwhile, the platform offers open application programming interfaces (APIs) for integration with existing Transportation Management Systems (TMS), Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) software and internal platforms. These connections allow companies to use Freightos’ pricing data, carrier connectivity and booking functions without replacing their existing technology infrastructure. Freightos also offers the platform as a data and execution engine for forwarders developing their own AI applications. The company said the upgraded system is designed to connect commercial decisions with shipment execution, from the initial customer enquiry through to confirmed booking. The next-generation Freightos for Forwarders platform is available globally, with modular integration options for freight forwarding companies.

articles.title: Ghana's oil & gas drilling yields hydrocarbons and first carbonate reservoir
articles.summary: This hydrocarbon discovery in a carbonate reservoir off Ghana's coast is unlocking new potential for the country’s upstream sector.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 11, 2026 · 9 minutes ago Ghana's oil & gas drilling yields hydrocarbons and first carbonate reservoir This hydrocarbon discovery in a carbonate reservoir off Ghana's coast is unlocking new potential for the country’s upstream sector. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email FPSO Kwame Nkrumah (for illustration purposes) Source: Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) A new discovery has been made at a deepwater exploration well off the coast of Ghana, marking the country's first successful test of a carbonate reservoir system and opening the door for a brand-new geological play that could help replenish dwindling reserves and attract fresh investment to the West African nation's energy industry. Planet One Oil & Gas , as the operator alongside its partners in the Deepwater Cape Three Points (DWCTP) Block , Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) and GOIL Upstream , has discovered hydrocarbons at the Nya Gyidie-1X exploration well offshore Ghana. GNPC describes the result as an important development in the country's efforts to find new petroleum resources to sustain future production, as this discovery establishes a new geological target for further exploration, beyond the sandstone reservoirs associated with the country's existing commercial oil and gas fields. Located approximately 148 kilometers off the coast of Ghana, Nya Gyidie-1X, which was drilled in water depths of 2,289 meters, encountered hydrocarbons in carbonate rock between 3,364 and 3,499 meters measured depth along the wellbore. According to Ghana National Petroleum Corporation, the result is particularly encouraging for Ghana's upstream petroleum industry, where replacing produced reserves, attracting fresh exploration investment, and addressing declining production remain important priorities. " The significance of Nya Gyidie-1X goes beyond the hydrocarbons encountered in this well. For the first time in Ghana, we have tested and confirmed hydrocarbons in a carbonate reservoir system, opening up a new geological play for further exploration. At a time when replenishing our reserves and sustaining production are national priorities, this is an encouraging development. The next task is to establish the scale and commercial potential of the discovery through rigorous technical evaluation. GNPC looks forward to working with Planet One and GOIL Upstream to build on this result and advance the development and production opportunities it presents for Ghana. " — Kwame Ntow Amoah GNPC's Chief Executive Related Articles Fossil Energy Four more wells set to come online in months ahead offshore Ghana 3 min read The company emphasizes that this discovery is expected to help consolidate the renewed wave of interest and investment in petroleum exploration and production, with a particular focus on identifying additional resources and improving the upstream sector's long-term outlook. Further technical work is required to determine the size, characteristics, and commercial viability of this discovery to guide subsequent exploration and appraisal decisions. The partners and the relevant regulatory institutions will evaluate the discovery to determine the next steps. The Planet One-operated DWCTP block was formally part of a larger acreage comprising the SDWT, GH-WB-02, 03, and 04, several of which remain available for licensing. Many international companies are investing in exploring Ghana’s hydrocarbon potential, as illustrated by Petrobras’ expression of interest in exploration blocks located in offshore areas of the country's Keta Basin. articles.title: RCL posts higher Q3 profit and orders 12 containerships
articles.summary: Regional Container Lines (RCL) reported a sharp increase in third-quarter profit as higher freight rates supported earnings despite lower container volumes. The Thailand-based shipping company recorded a net profit of THB 3.26 billion for the three months ended 30 September 2026. This represents a 64.7% increase from...
articles.body: Regional Container Lines (RCL) reported a sharp increase in third-quarter profit as higher freight rates supported earnings despite lower container volumes. The Thailand-based shipping company recorded a net profit of THB 3.26 billion for the three months ended 30 September 2026. This represents a 64.7% increase from THB 1.98 billion in the previous quarter. Freight income rose by THB 1.05 billion, or 10.4%, compared with the second quarter. Meanwhile, freight and operating costs declined by 2.4%, supporting the improvement in profitability. However, total container liftings fell by 4.1% during the quarter. RCL attributed the stronger earnings partly to higher freight rates caused by congestion at major ports and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The company’s average freight rate increased from US$552 per TEU in the second quarter to US$624 per TEU in the third quarter. Higher freight rates offset lower volumes For the first nine months of 2026, RCL reported a net profit of THB 6.91 billion, up 8.6% from THB 6.36 billion in the corresponding period last year. Freight income increased by 7.5%, supported by a rise in average freight rates from US$420 to US$520 per TEU. Nevertheless, container liftings declined by 232,000 TEU, or 11.7%, compared with the first nine months of 2025. According to RCL, congestion at ports in Asia and Europe extended vessel waiting times and voyage durations. As a result, ships completed fewer round voyages, reducing the overall volume of containers transported. The company also identified disruption linked to the Middle East conflict and shortages of containers across global shipping networks. To manage these conditions, RCL adjusted vessel routes to avoid conflict areas. It also shifted capacity towards trade lanes with stronger demand to maintain fleet utilisation. RCL orders 12 new container vessels Alongside its financial results, RCL confirmed orders for 12 new containerships during the third quarter of 2026. The programme includes four vessels with a capacity of 1,900 TEU each, six vessels of 3,100 TEU and two larger ships of 9,200 TEU. Together, the newbuildings represent 44,600 TEU of additional nominal capacity. Deliveries are scheduled to begin in 2028. RCL said the vessels will support its network expansion and strengthen its service capabilities. The company has not disclosed the shipyards involved or the total value of the orders in its latest financial statement. Meanwhile, RCL continues to introduce vessels from its existing 4,488 TEU newbuilding programme. In September, the company held a naming ceremony in Guangzhou for Anitta Bhum , Benyapar Bhum and Chantisa Bhum . As previously reported by Container News , Anitta Bhum was delivered in September and assigned to the carrier’s East Asia–Latin America network. RCL also declared an interim dividend of THB 0.50 per share, with payment scheduled for 4 December 2026.

The Thailand-based shipping company recorded a net profit of THB 3.26 billion for the three months ended 30 September 2026.

articles.title: Coal’s new world order takes shape
articles.summary: Coal’s changing trade map is creating winners and losers across dry bulk shipping in 2026, with Indonesian exports retreating, southern African shipments setting records and Asian import demand increasingly fractured. Clarksons Research forecasts seaborne coal trade will edge up just 1% this year to 1.343bn tonnes....
articles.body: Dry Cargo Coal’s new world order takes shape Sam Chambers November 11, 2026 0 373 1 minute read Coal’s changing trade map is creating winners and losers across dry bulk shipping in 2026, with Indonesian exports retreating, southern African shipments setting records and Asian import demand increasingly fractured. Clarksons Research forecasts seaborne coal trade will edge up just 1% this year to 1.343bn tonnes. Beneath that modest increase, Indonesian exports are projected to fall 6% to 496.9m tonnes, while Australian shipments climb 4% to 371.3m tonnes. Chinese seaborne imports are expected to decline 5%, India’s 3%, while Japan’s rise 3%. The Indonesian retreat is already evident on loading lists. Braemar’s analysis of AXSMarine tracking shows exports falling 8% year-on-year during January-October. Capesize shipments were down 24%, supramax and ultramax movements 12%, and panamax cargoes 4%. Export procedures and low river levels have compounded pressure on shipments. Southern Africa presents a contrast. Ursa Shipbrokers calculates combined South African and Mozambican steam coal exports reached a ten-year high of 64.92m tonnes during January-October, with 27.26m tonnes destined for India. Globally, however, tracked seaborne steam coal trade fell 1.5% to 801.1m tonnes, including a 7.9% decline in Indonesian shipments. India offers perhaps the year’s biggest paradox. BIMCO reports coal imports dropped 7% in the first ten months despite coal-fired electricity generation rising around 9%. Expensive imported supplies have encouraged greater reliance on domestic production and stock drawdowns. BRS says coal inventories at power stations were equivalent to only 5.9 days of consumption, against 14.7 days a year earlier. Supramaxes have been hardest hit, with Indian-bound coal volumes falling 16%, compared with a 4% decline for panamaxes. October offered the first signs of a turn, with Indian seaborne coal arrivals rising 7% year-on-year. However, BIMCO expects only a limited import recovery in 2027 as domestic mining grows. The Middle East energy crisis has meanwhile encouraged coal-fired generation in parts of Europe and northeast Asia as LNG supplies tightened. The changing dynamics of global coal trades will come under the spotlight at Geneva Dry 2027 next April, where panellists, including Danilo Fumarola, CEO of Gestion Maritime Group, and Peter Weernink, chairman of SwissMarine, will examine shifting tonne-mile patterns, the routes gaining ground, China’s appetite for coal imports and whether the fallout from the war around the Strait of Hormuz will have a lasting impact on demand. articles.body: Europe Operations Ukrainian drones strike major Russian Baltic export port Sam Chambers November 11, 2026 0 489 1 minute read X.com X.com Ukraine has launched a major drone attack on Russia’s Baltic port of Ust-Luga, setting fire to port infrastructure, injuring three workers and disrupting power supplies. Leningrad region governor Alexander Drozdenko confirmed early Wednesday that several drones had struck the port area, triggering a fire and an emergency shutdown of a transformer substation. Three port workers were injured, although their injuries were not life-threatening, according to the governor. Ust-Luga is among Russia’s most important Baltic export gateways, handling crude oil, refined petroleum products, coal, grain and other bulk commodities. The extent of damage to individual terminals remains unclear, with no confirmation yet of suspended loading operations or vessels being struck. The attack comes just two days after Ukrainian drones hit the Kirishi refinery, Russia’s second-largest, also in the Leningrad region. The Surgutneftegaz-operated facility, which has annual processing capacity of around 20m tonnes, caught fire following Monday’s attack. Ukraine’s intensifying campaign against Russian refining infrastructure is beginning to have wider repercussions. The Financial Times reported yesterday that Rosneft has introduced petrol rationing at filling stations as refinery outages and fuel shortages mount. The latest Baltic attack follows another violent weekend in the Black Sea. Splash reported on Monday that Russia had claimed fresh attacks on merchant ships around Odesa and Chornomorsk, although the incidents could not be independently verified. The European Commission announced €50m ($58m) in funding this week to accelerate a maritime security hub in Romania and Bulgaria following a series of deadly attacks on commercial shipping. articles.title: NYSHEX raises US$8.7 million to expand NYFI freight index
articles.summary: New York Shipping Exchange (NYSHEX) has raised US$8.7 million in Series D funding to expand its NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) and strengthen its container shipping risk management services. The financing round was led by NewRoad Capital Partners and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), with participation from existing...
articles.body: New York Shipping Exchange (NYSHEX) has raised US$8.7 million in Series D funding to expand its NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) and strengthen its container shipping risk management services. The financing round was led by NewRoad Capital Partners and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), with participation from existing investors. As part of the investment, Stuart Williams, Chief Operating Officer of ICE, will join the NYSHEX Board of Directors. The funding will support the expansion of NYFI into additional markets. NYSHEX also plans to develop more detailed freight benchmarks and improve analytics linked to exchange-traded freight futures. NYFI expansion targets freight market transparency According to the official NYSHEX announcement , the company will focus on broader geographic coverage and greater detail in its container freight indices. Launched in April 2025, NYFI uses freight rates from shipments that have actually moved rather than relying on quoted or booked rates. This approach provides market participants with benchmarks based on completed shipping transactions. ICE administers the index and has listed four futures contracts linked to NYFI during 2026. These contracts cover major container shipping routes connecting Asia with the United States and Europe. The contracts allow market participants to manage exposure to changes in freight rates. Shippers can use these instruments to address rising transportation costs, while carriers and freight forwarders can manage risks associated with market fluctuations. The NYFI has also been available through Container News since July 2026, providing readers with access to transaction-based container freight benchmarks. NYSHEX plans to use the new funding to expand the index’s coverage and develop additional analytical capabilities around the listed contracts. ICE strengthens investment and board representation The Series D round deepens the relationship between NYSHEX and ICE, which previously participated in the company’s Series C financing in 2024. In addition to its investment, ICE will gain representation on the NYSHEX board through Stuart Williams. Gordon Downes, CEO and co-founder of NYSHEX, said the financing would support the development of tools that help the shipping industry manage freight rate volatility. “Our investors are backing that direction, and this funding goes into building it out,” said Downes. Williams highlighted the importance of using actual shipping transactions as the basis for freight benchmarks. He also noted that NYFI-linked futures complement ICE’s existing tanker freight and bunker fuel markets. Beyond the index itself, NYSHEX will continue developing software for shippers, carriers and freight forwarders. These products support shipment planning, contract execution and the management of supply chain risks. The company currently serves more than 200 shippers, shipping lines and freight forwarders worldwide. NYSHEX has not announced a timetable for the additional geographic indices or new analytical features planned under the funding programme.

According to a statement carried by Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, the vessel caught fire after attempting to use what Tehran described as an unauthorised shipping route. The IRGC claimed that damage to American coastal radar and navigational systems had increased the dangers facing vessels navigating outside Iranian-designated routes. The claims could not be independently verified, and Tehran provided no vessel names, casualty figures or supporting evidence. The latest incidents follow a particularly violent weekend in which multiple tankers were attacked around Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, including one vessel that caught fire and required its crew to be evacuated. articles.summary: More than 30 maritime organisations have joined forces at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey to push for electricity to account for at least 20% of international shipping’s energy consumption by 2035. The Maritime Electrification Breakthrough Goal, launched yesterday in Antalya by the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF)...
articles.body: Bunkering Environment Tech Maritime coalition targets 20% electrification by 2035 Sam Chambers November 11, 2026 0 274 1 minute read Maritime Battery Forum Maritime Battery Forum More than 30 maritime organisations have joined forces at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey to push for electricity to account for at least 20% of international shipping’s energy consumption by 2035. The Maritime Electrification Breakthrough Goal, launched yesterday in Antalya by the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF) and RMI, has attracted support from organisations including the Port of Long Beach, Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) and Maritime Battery Forum. The target equates to approximately two exajoules, or 556 terawatt-hours, of electricity annually — equivalent to more than a year’s electricity consumption in France — underlining the enormous investment in power generation, port infrastructure and charging facilities that would be required. More than 1,600 electric and hybrid vessels are already operating worldwide, according to Maritime Battery Forum figures cited by the coalition. Research highlighted in the initiative suggests vessel segments representing around 30% of maritime energy consumption could be technically electrified by 2030, with electrification potentially economically attractive for 90% of that technically suitable fleet. The coalition is calling for greater investment in port electricity infrastructure, power grids and renewable generation, alongside stronger regulatory incentives from the International Maritime Organization. However, the target remains voluntary, with delivery dependent on coordinated investment by shipowners, ports, utilities and governments. The initiative forms part of COP31’s wider ambition to increase electricity’s share of global final energy demand to 35% by 2035. Its launch comes ahead of renewed IMO negotiations later this month over the organisation’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, with discussions scheduled to resume in London on November 23. articles.body: Americas Containers Dry Cargo Gas Tankers Panama Canal turns the taps back on Sam Chambers November 11, 2026 0 511 1 minute read Panama Canal Authority Panama Canal Authority The Panama Canal has raised its daily transit capacity to 34 vessels and increased the maximum allowable draft for neopanamax ships to 50 ft, marking another significant easing of restrictions following an exceptionally wet October. The Panama Canal Authority (ACP) confirmed that an additional booking slot for super-category vessels at the original panamax locks would increase their daily allocation from 18 to 19. Total availability now stands at 24 slots through the panamax locks and 10 through the larger neopanamax locks, up from a combined 33 previously. Rainfall across the canal watershed during the first 29 days of October was 8.4% above the 30-year average and 83.6% greater than the corresponding period three years ago. The turnaround is particularly striking given the dire outlook during August, when weak rainfall and a strengthening El Niño forced authorities to slash daily booking capacity to 32 vessels and impose tighter draft restrictions. The restrictions had driven competition for guaranteed passages to extraordinary levels, with Splash reporting a record $5.3m auction payment by an LPG carrier for a September transit. The partnership pairs an affordable, expendable strike system with a reusable surface vessel that can return to port, refuel, and reload. Both companies design for production at scale, supported by resilient domestic and allied supply chains, so the capability can be fielded and sustained in numbers. articles.body: Konecranes has secured an order for a Gottwald ESP.4 Mobile Harbor Crane from Stevedoring Services Limited (SSL) in Bermuda, marking the model’s first order outside Europe. The Finnish equipment manufacturer booked the order during the third quarter of 2026. Delivery is scheduled for the third quarter of 2027. SSL plans to use the new crane primarily for container handling operations. The equipment will also provide additional lifting capacity for general and project cargo. The order represents another step in the company’s equipment modernisation programme, following the delivery of an earlier-generation Konecranes Gottwald crane in 2011. New crane to support container operations The Gottwald ESP.4 is the smallest model in Konecranes’ Generation 6 range, which the company expanded with the introduction of the ESP.4 earlier this year. Designed for smaller ports, the crane combines a compact structure with high lifting speeds and flexible cargo handling capabilities. It offers a maximum lifting capacity of 100 tonnes, compared with 60 tonnes for SSL’s existing Gottwald HMK 170 E crane. The new model also has a maximum working radius of 42 metres and hoisting speeds of up to 120 metres per minute. These capabilities are expected to support faster container handling while allowing SSL to accommodate a wider range of heavy and project cargo. Randy Rochester, CEO of Stevedoring Services Limited, said the company selected the equipment because of its lifting performance, operating speed and suitability for Bermuda’s port infrastructure. He also highlighted SSL’s positive experience with its existing Konecranes crane and the manufacturer’s technical support. Meanwhile, Alan Garcia, Vice President Regional Sales Americas at Konecranes Port Solutions, described the Bermuda order as an opportunity to introduce the ESP.4 to additional port operators outside Europe. The model also incorporates digital tools and smart features developed for the company’s Generation 6 mobile harbor crane range. According to Konecranes, the order reflects demand for equipment that can improve cargo handling flexibility without requiring the space associated with larger crane models. The company has not disclosed the contract value. The operational benefits will depend on the crane’s deployment following its planned delivery in 2027.

articles.body: Drewry Shipping Consultants has partnered with ocean freight management platform Cargoo to integrate freight benchmarking data into its digital procurement system. The agreement allows customers who use Cargoo and belong to the Drewry Benchmarking Club to access their benchmark data directly within the platform. The integration connects market rate information with freight procurement, carrier negotiations and contract management. It aims to help shippers compare offers and monitor transportation costs throughout the contract period. However, access is limited to Drewry Benchmarking Club members who are also Cargoo customers. Benchmark data supports freight negotiations Through the integration, eligible shippers can compare carrier quotations with Drewry’s benchmark rates for individual trade lanes. The platform displays both the lowest and average benchmark rates. It also provides access to container shipping forecasts covering seven quarters. These figures can help procurement teams set rate targets before launching tenders. They can then compare incoming offers against market benchmarks during each bidding round. The system also links tender results with carrier contracts and shipment bookings. According to Drewry’s announcement, Cargoo checks bookings against the agreed contract rates. Its freight auditing functions also review invoice charges while disputes can still be raised. This approach allows shippers to use benchmarking information beyond the initial negotiation stage. Tender preparation remains a challenge The partnership comes as shipping companies and cargo owners prepare for upcoming freight contract negotiations. Recent Drewry Benchmarking Club polls show that 44% of participating members need five to seven weeks to prepare a request for quotation (RFQ). Meanwhile, half of respondents reported needing eight to twelve weeks to complete the full bidding process. The surveys also found that one in four members could not identify their annual detention and demurrage expenditure. These findings highlight the difficulties procurement teams face when collecting shipment data, reviewing carrier proposals and tracking freight costs. The integration is designed to address some of these challenges by combining benchmark rates, tender management and shipment execution in one system. Cargoo’s platform connects procurement decisions with capacity allocations, carrier contracts and bookings. It also uses shipment performance and spending data to support future tender planning. Drewry has previously highlighted the importance of stronger contract terms and freight rate benchmarking when negotiating ocean freight agreements. The companies have not disclosed the number of customers using the new integration or any measured cost savings resulting from its introduction.

The Japanese engineering group reported net sales of ¥175 billion ($1.15 billion) for the six months ended 30 September 2026, an increase of 5.7% year on year. The company attributed the decrease mainly to large contracts secured in Southeast Asia and the United States during the corresponding period last year. articles.title: USCG Warns Shipowners to Verify Air Draft, Avoid Bridge Strike
articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) has issued a Marine Safety Alert warning vessel owners, operators and crews to verify their ships' maximum air draft before transiting beneath bridges and other overhead obstructions, following an incident in which…
articles.body: USCG Warns Shipowners to Verify Air Draft, Avoid Bridge Strike Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 copyright karegg/AdobeStock The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) has issued a Marine Safety Alert warning vessel owners, operators and crews to verify their ships' maximum air draft before transiting beneath bridges and other overhead obstructions, following an incident in which an unaccounted-for antenna struck a bridge. In Safety Alert 17-26, issued November 10, 2026, the Coast Guard detailed its investigation of a deep-draft vessel that contacted a bridge despite voyage-planning calculations indicating sufficient vertical clearance. Investigators determined that the vessel's reported air draft was based on outdated plans that did not reflect its current configuration. Multiple versions of the ship's plans were maintained on board, and the documents used to calculate air draft failed to account for an installed MF/HF tiltable antenna extending above the vessel's reported highest point. Because the antenna was omitted from the calculation, the crew did not recognize the need to lower it before passing beneath the bridge. The vessel's pilot subsequently received an understated air-draft figure, creating a false margin of safety during transit planning. The incident highlights the risks associated with vessel modifications and equipment installations that alter a ship's vertical profile without corresponding updates to technical documentation and operating procedures. The Coast Guard recommends that shipowners and operators incorporate air-draft verification into their safety management systems, maintain current vessel-specific drawings, and clearly identify or remove superseded documentation. Operators should also establish procedures for configuring movable equipment before overhead-clearance transits and require positive confirmation that antennas and other adjustable structures are properly lowered or secured. The alert was developed by USCG Sector Los Angeles–Long Beach and distributed by the Coast Guard's Office of Investigations and Casualty Analysis.

The event was chaired by Mar Chao, President of Valenciaport, and Sam Liu, Vice...
articles.body: Valenciaport and Shanghai International Port Group held a joint presentation for their clients at the Shanghai Tower, aimed at showing the business opportunities between the two ports and strengthening cooperation on green corridors. The event was chaired by Mar Chao, President of Valenciaport, and Sam Liu, Vice President of SIPG, and was joined by Guoqiang Shi, CEO of CSP Spain. China is Valenciaport’s largest international market for container traffic. Between January and September 2026, 714,691 TEUs were handled in trade with China, up 15.07% on the same period last year, while cargo tonnage reached 7.66 million tonnes, up 15.75%. The Port of Shanghai accounts for 36 percent of Valenciaport’s trade with China, equal to 2.3 million tonnes a year. Chao described Valenciaport’s position in the Western Mediterranean as making it one of the main gateways for goods moving between Asia, Spain and the rest of Europe, with more than 100 regular shipping services linking it to all five continents. The visit aimed to give Chinese companies first-hand knowledge of what Valenciaport offers as an entry point to the Spanish and European markets, including strong maritime connectivity, rail links to major logistics and industrial hubs, and a hinterland covering a large share of Spain’s economy. Valenciaport handles more than 40% of Spain’s total import and export traffic. She called the port a reliable and competitive partner for Chinese companies’ international growth, and said there is great potential for further collaboration. Digitalisation, innovation and sustainability are the three areas where the Port Authority wants to deepen cooperation with China, since ports will increasingly compete on efficiency, connectivity and the ability to build smarter, more sustainable logistics chains. Valenciaport has long been digitalising its operations and advancing its energy transition. Its Net Zero Emissions Plan targets net zero by the middle of the next decade, with electrification, renewable energy and shore power for vessels already under way. Chao also attended the China International Import Expo in Shanghai, where she met representatives of the Chinese logistics, port and business communities to strengthen Valenciaport’s visibility and positioning in the region.

articles.summary: The Trump administration has formally extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months, keeping the controversial measures on hold while Washington continues trade...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Port of Long Beach The Trump administration has formally extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months, keeping the controversial measures on hold while Washington continues trade negotiations with Beijing. The decision, published Tuesday in the Federal Register, extends the suspension through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on January 9, 2027, with the measures potentially resuming January 10 unless further action is taken. The extension took effect November 9, preventing the fees from returning following the expiration of an earlier one-year suspension agreed to under a trade deal between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in November 2025. Under the notice issued by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR), shipping companies will not accrue liability for or be required to pay the maritime transport fees established under the administration’s Section 301 investigation into China’s dominance of the maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors. The extension also maintains the suspension of additional duties on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes and other cargo-handling equipment. The measures were originally adopted in April 2025 and subsequently modified in October 2025 as part of a broader effort to counter China’s growing influence over global shipbuilding and maritime transportation. The administration initially suspended the measures for one year beginning November 10, 2025, following a trade agreement between Trump and Xi. The latest extension provides another two months for negotiations. USTR said the circumstances that justified the original suspension remain in place, with discussions between the two countries continuing. The decision follows an October 26 proposal to extend the suspension, which drew approximately 60 unique public comments. According to USTR, supporters argued that keeping the measures on hold would prevent higher shipping costs, avoid commercial disruptions and provide additional time for negotiations with China. Opponents, however, warned that suspending the fees would weaken incentives to invest in American shipbuilding and related industries, potentially allowing China’s dominance of the sector to grow. Other commenters urged the administration to permanently eliminate certain maritime service fees, citing potential disruptions to U.S. exports. Some also called for the tariffs on Chinese cargo-handling equipment to be considered separately from the vessel fees. Despite the extension, USTR emphasized that rebuilding American shipbuilding capacity remains a priority. During the suspension, the administration said it would continue working to expand domestic commercial shipbuilding, develop a more resilient maritime workforce and coordinate with allies to strengthen U.S. shipbuilding capabilities. The extension also leaves open the possibility that the fees could return early next year. USTR said it will continue monitoring China’s maritime and shipbuilding practices and consider whether to extend the suspension again or take further action before the January 10 deadline. The decision comes as China has also extended its suspension of retaliatory port fees targeting U.S.-linked vessels until January 10, 2027, according to a Reuters report on Monday. China also extended its suspension of an investigation into the security of shipping and shipbuilding supply chains. articles.title: Port of Brunswick Expands Auto Shipping Capacity as Georgia Manufacturing Booms
articles.summary: The Georgia Ports Authority is expanding automotive shipping capacity at the Port of Brunswick as a growing number of global automakers establish manufacturing operations across the state, strengthening Georgia’s position...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Port of Brunswick The Georgia Ports Authority is expanding automotive shipping capacity at the Port of Brunswick as a growing number of global automakers establish manufacturing operations across the state, strengthening Georgia’s position as a major hub for vehicle production and logistics. At its annual State of the Port of Brunswick event on Tuesday, port officials highlighted new automotive investments, rising demand for roll-on/roll-off (RoRo) shipping and a nearly $5 billion infrastructure investment program planned over the next decade. The Port of Brunswick, which the authority identifies as a U.S. leader in automotive imports and exports, has experienced 277% growth over the past decade, according to the authority. Its three RoRo berths at Colonel’s Island handled 50 vessels in October alone. A fourth RoRo berth is now 60% complete and scheduled to open in December 2027. The expansion will increase capacity and accommodate newer generations of vehicle carriers capable of transporting more than 10,800 car equivalent units (CEUs). The additional berth is expected to improve vessel turnaround times while providing room for future growth in vehicle imports and exports. “Georgia Ports are creating opportunities for businesses to grow, enhancing long-term supply chain competitiveness on a state, regional, national and global level, generating new job growth in the port region and throughout the state,” said Georgia Ports Authority CEO Griff Lynch. The expansion comes as Georgia attracts billions of dollars in automotive manufacturing investment. Hyundai Motor Group’s 3,000-acre Metaplant near Savannah is expected to create 8,500 jobs by 2031 and has attracted 22 nearby suppliers. Kia has operated its manufacturing plant in West Point since 2009, while electric vehicle maker Rivian is developing a $5 billion manufacturing facility at Stanton Springs North, expected to create 7,500 long-term jobs by 2030. More recently, Audi announced plans to establish its first U.S. manufacturing plant near Macon, Georgia. The German automaker intends to invest $4 billion in the facility, creating approximately 4,500 jobs. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027, with production expected in the early 2030s. Other major automakers, including BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Volvo, already use Brunswick for finished-vehicle shipments and processing. Georgia Ports Authority President Kevin Price said the state’s expanding automotive manufacturing base is also supporting growth in other cargo segments. “The automotive manufacturing ecosystem continues to grow here. We’re also seeing strong growth in the heavy machinery market such as construction equipment and farm equipment,” Price said. While Brunswick handles finished vehicles and heavy equipment, the Port of Savannah serves as a major gateway for containerized automotive parts and components. According to the authority, Savannah handles approximately 40 vessel calls per week, 15,000 daily truck gate transactions and 42 double-stack trains weekly through its Mason Mega Rail facility, connecting the port to inland markets via Norfolk Southern and CSX. The Georgia Ports Authority’s nearly $5 billion investment plan includes five additional container ship berths in Savannah and the fourth RoRo berth in Brunswick. Over the past decade, the authority’s board has approved $4.13 billion in infrastructure improvements. The investments are intended to position Georgia’s ports for continued growth in automotive manufacturing, vehicle exports and imports, and containerized trade as manufacturers expand their U.S. operations. articles.title: ‘Nonsense Rate’: Iran War Exposes Turmoil Behind Key Tanker Benchmark
articles.summary: In March this year, inside a 282-year-old institution responsible for one of the most important prices in global oil markets, one man staged a quiet protest.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche By Jack Farchy and Alex Longley (Bloomberg) — In March this year, inside a 282-year-old institution responsible for one of the most important prices in global oil markets, one man staged a quiet protest. “Nonsense rate,” Christopher Loveday wrote on March 23 in an internal document at the Baltic Exchange, where he was responsible for helping produce the world’s benchmark rate for shipping oil. “Still a nonsense,” he wrote two days later. On March 31, as he filled in his section of the spreadsheet that sets the price of a benchmark underpinning billions of dollars in freight derivatives trading, he wrote: “b/s rate.” The comments are among numerous internal communications, emails and calls that have become public in filings and court testimony during a legal battle playing out in London between the Baltic and oil trader Mercuria Energy Group. Collectively, they offer unprecedented insight into how the war in Iran played out inside a key corner of the global oil market. In particular, the case has provided a fly-on-the-wall perspective on events inside the Baltic, which for centuries has been at the heart of the global shipping industry. It has shown that numerous people involved in the key oil tanker rate, called TD3C, expressed reservations as the Baltic Exchange continued to publish the price in the early weeks of the war. It has put a spotlight on the Baltic’s guidance allowing for derivatives contracts underpinned by TD3C to be used in setting the benchmark itself, which was met with shocked derision by some of the industry’s biggest players. And it has shown tensions running high within the Baltic’s senior staff, with one describing the company as “so rotten.” It’s unclear how the revelations, while embarrassing for the Baltic and its owner Singapore Exchange Ltd., will affect the outcome of the case. Lawyers for the two sides are due to make their closing arguments in court this week, after which the judge could take several months to come to a decision. Mercuria, whose demands have changed several times since it launched the case in April, is seeking to have the judge declare that the Baltic was wrong to keep publishing the TD3C index in the initial phase of the war from March to July. “This is obviously a difficult moment for the Baltic, and it’s important for the market that it comes through this and learns whatever it needs to learn,” said Halvor Ellefsen, a London-based director at Fearnleys Shipbrokers UK Ltd. “Any commodity market needs reliable benchmarks and freight is integral to that.” The Baltic has argued its decision was justified and that, in any case, any breaches of its obligations should be addressed by its regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, rather than in private legal action. It declined to comment for this story while the trial continues. Not an Exchange The Baltic Exchange’s history dates back to 1744, when it was formally established in Threadneedle Street as the Virginia and Baltick Coffee House as a venue for trading commodities — key among them tallow from the Baltic Sea region. While a key cog in global shipping and commodity markets, the institution employed just over 30 people last year and made a pre-tax profit of £379,000, according to its most recent annual accounts. Its offices are in the heart of the City of London, a short walk from the Tower of London. And despite its name, the Baltic Exchange today is not actually an exchange at all: its main role is to collect assessments from a small group of brokers to produce benchmark indexes for the price of shipping. When the US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, Loveday’s role was to oversee that process for the Baltic’s most important tanker index: TD3C, which represents the cost of hiring a very large crude carrier, or VLCC, on the route from Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia to Ningbo in China. Every day, he would review the numbers submitted by the nine broker “panelists” responsible for assessing the TD3C rate, question any that seemed out of whack to him, and also insert his own estimate of the rate into the Baltic’s spreadsheet — to serve as a sense-checking reference point for comparing the brokers’ numbers. The TD3C index is published just after 4 p.m. every day, using an average of the panelists’ assessments. The crucial question for the Baltic staff in the first days of the war was whether TD3C should be suspended. Over three weeks of hearings, Mercuria’s legal team has argued that the Baltic got the answer wrong. At 9:15 a.m. on the morning of March 2, the first working day after the war began, the Baltic’s small team held a call, according to Loveday’s witness statement. Several of their key routes, including TD3C, involved transiting the Strait of Hormuz — something ships had abruptly stopped doing over the weekend. At that point it was unclear how long the war would last, or whether it would have a lasting impact on the flow of oil. Over the following week, the Baltic had numerous interactions with brokers, traders and shipowners. Tanker traffic through the Strait had all but ceased, and several traders argued that the TD3C rates should be suspended (though Mercuria was not among them — it advocated instead for basing TD3C on alternative routes that were still operating normally). Draft Notice Mark Jackson, a shipping industry veteran who had been CEO of the Baltic since 2017, even commissioned a draft notice announcing the suspension of all rates on routes involving the Strait of Hormuz, he said in his witness statement. Still, there were hopes that the war may end quickly, and when the Baltic held a call for its panelist brokers on March 4, the conclusion was that they were willing to keep submitting assessments. TD3C would continue. Yet Loveday, the Baltic employee most directly responsible for the TD3C process, stopped inputting his own estimates into the Baltic’s spreadsheet. In fact, it was only after the Baltic received a complaint and its head of compliance started looking into TD3C, that Loveday’s boss noticed the missing numbers and told him to restart, according to witness statements from the Baltic executives. Loveday, who worked as a shipbroker for about 28 years before joining the Baltic in 2019, registered his protest in the notes of the spreadsheet. “I don’t see how we can possibly report here,” he wrote on March 20. (He later explained in his witness statement that this had been written while he was waiting for a flight at Houston airport and was “feeling a little ‘non-compliant’.”) He continued to insert snide comments until early April, when a colleague took over as the assessor of TD3C. In his witness statement, Loveday said that his comments were specifically about the futility of his own attempts to estimate the rate, rather than about the benchmark itself. Still, he also said in court that he had thought since the start of the war that TD3C should have been suspended. And Loveday was not the only person involved in the production of TD3C to express concerns. One Baltic staffer said in early April that the rate was “starting to lose credibility”; another told colleagues that if he was not at the Baltic he would have “zero confidence” in the rate, according to transcripts of internal calls cited by Mercuria’s lawyers. When the Baltic convened the panelists on March 16, several argued in favor of a suspension. “It’s purely hypothetical…I think it’s just complete nonsense, the whole thing,” one said. One panelist refused to submit assessments for several weeks, while two other panelists submitted the same value every day for weeks at a time. Still, the Baltic continued to publish the index. It has argued that it was led by the panelists – the brokers with the most information about what tanker deals were being discussed – and that at no point did a majority of them say they couldn’t assess the rate. ‘Extraordinary Circumstances’ Besides continuing to publish TD3C itself, one of the more controversial decisions to emerge from the court proceedings was a piece of guidance issued by the Baltic Exchange, to help the broker panelists to arrive at their assessments of the market. In “extraordinary circumstances,” the Baltic wrote in early March, panelists could base their judgment of the tanker market by looking at price levels in the shipping derivatives contracts – known as forward freight agreements – that were themselves underpinned by TD3C. The inclusion of the reference to the FFA market received an immediate backlash. TD3C was supposed to be based on actual deals being done and discussed in the real world. If TD3C could be set based on movements in the derivatives market, the whole system risked losing touch with reality. “You are literally leaving your index open for direct abuse,” one trader wrote to the Baltic of the decision. “It’s like having a criminal write his own sentence.” When one panelist wrote in the Baltic’s spreadsheet of assessments that they had used the FFA market as a guide, Baltic CEO Jackson told a colleague they should be careful that information “doesn’t get out.” (Jackson said in court that he had simply wanted to avoid further discussions on the subject, though he agreed with Mercuria’s barrister that the comment didn’t reflect the Baltic’s motto “Our Word Our Bond.”) The Baltic has defended its instructions to panelists that they can use the FFA market as a reference point – and indeed the guidance still stands, one of the Baltic’s senior assessors confirmed to the court. In court filings, expert witnesses from the two sides said that physical and FFA markets may inform one another, but noted that FFA information “should not be used as the sole determinant of a physical TD3C assessment.” Freight Surge | Daily earnings for supertankers jumped because of Iran war The significance of the huge derivatives market underpinned by TD3C — worth 17.4 billion euros ($19.4 billion) in the first six months of this year — was highlighted in court for both the Baltic and Mercuria. Mercuria was the largest user of TD3C derivatives, accounting for between 25% and 50% of total open interest, according to its freight derivatives trader David Schickler. It was generally short TD3C derivatives as a hedge for the earnings of its fleet of oil tankers around the world. When the TD3C rates soared at the start of the war, Mercuria’s derivatives positions faced hefty losses. But the company’s tankers didn’t experience a similar surge in earnings, and its traders testified that they weren’t able to sail through Hormuz to take advantage of the high rates supposedly on offer. Mercuria has said its losses as a result of the mismatch were likely to be in the hundreds of millions of dollars, although it has removed that claim from its most recent legal filings. When the Baltic’s lawyer asked Renaud Hauspy, a freight trader at Mercuria, if the effect of Mercuria’s index-linked position had been a “disaster,” Hauspy replied: “It has not been positive.” Mercuria’s lawyers, meanwhile, argued that the size of the FFA market was part of the reason that it kept publishing the benchmark. In a mid-April call, Matthew Cox, the Baltic’s head of benchmark production, asked: “Would we have suspended TD3 had it not been for the open interest, had it not been for the FFAs? And I think had it, you know, had TD3 been a, any other index, we would, we would have, um, suspended.” (Cox told the court that he was incorrect to suggest that every other criterion for suspension had been met.) As the weeks dragged on, frustrations continued to grow inside the Baltic. In one internal call that was read out in court by a lawyer for Mercuria, one of the Baltic’s assessors described the company as “so rotten at the moment.” Since the Baltic’s head of compliance started her job in April 2022, she has received four formal complaints: all of them since the Iran war began, and all of them about TD3C, she said in her witness statement. The most recent of them, on August 12, was from Mercuria itself. Mercuria initially sought in its lawsuit to have TD3C retroactively suspended, but has adjusted its claim multiple times, most recently seeking only that the court rule the Baltic should have suspended the route from March until July. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has picked up sharply during the second half of the year despite the ongoing conflict, with exports from countries other than Iran recently nearing prewar levels. But the trade has remained shrouded in secrecy. And it has increasingly become dominated by one company: Sinokor, which accounted for more than 50% of all transits since early July along the “southern” route by the Omani coast, according to a report produced for the case by maritime security company Ambrey. It’s far from clear that the difficulties assessing tanker rates have gone away. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. REUTERS/Steve Nesius/File Photo The U.S. Department of Energy has closed a $480 million loan to modernize 22 offshore platforms in the Gulf of Mexico, marking the department’s first completed loan financing domestic oil and natural gas production. The financing, announced Tuesday, will support Arena Energy’s Project Elkhorn, a major infrastructure redevelopment effort in the Southern Eugene Island area off Louisiana. The project is expected to increase offshore production by as much as 38,600 barrels of oil and 77 million cubic feet of natural gas per day at peak output. The loan comes through the Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF), formerly known as the Loan Programs Office, which the Trump administration has redirected toward expanding domestic energy production and strengthening existing infrastructure. The Energy Department said the financing was made possible by provisions in President Donald Trump’s Working Families Tax Cut legislation. Arena Energy’s wholly owned subsidiary, Elkhorn Offshore, will use the financing to refurbish and reactivate idled platforms, expand production and water-handling capacity at existing facilities, and develop new natural gas pipeline infrastructure connecting future wells to existing gathering systems. Over the project’s operating life, Arena estimates the improvements could unlock approximately 125 million barrels of additional oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas. “The Southern Eugene Island area is one of the most prolific oil-producing regions in American history, and its infrastructure still has decades of productive life ahead,” said Mike Minarovic, Arena Energy’s founder and CEO. “What it needed was long-term capital to match the opportunity.” The financing represents a notable shift in the federal government’s approach to energy infrastructure lending. Previously known as the Loan Programs Office, the DOE financing program became a major source of federal support for clean energy projects, including renewable power, battery manufacturing and electric vehicles. Under the Trump administration, the renamed office has placed greater emphasis on conventional energy production, grid reliability and reinvestment in existing infrastructure. The Arena loan is the first to reach financial close specifically supporting domestic oil and gas production under the department’s lending programs, according to DOE. “The United States is the world’s largest producer and exporter of oil and natural gas, and thanks to President Trump, American energy production will continue to grow,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said. “Project Elkhorn will increase oil production by up to 38,600 barrels per day and create thousands of jobs,” Wright added. Arena currently produces approximately 30,000 barrels of oil per day from its offshore Gulf operations, according to DOE. The projected increase from Project Elkhorn would therefore represent a substantial expansion relative to the company’s existing oil production. The project is also expected to support 2,800 jobs, including 2,400 construction positions and 400 operations roles. Arena estimates the additional production will generate approximately $1.6 billion in federal royalty revenue over the life of the project, although that figure represents the company’s projection rather than a guaranteed return on the government’s financing. Founded in 1999, Arena Energy is among the largest privately held offshore oil and natural gas producers in the Gulf. The company says it has invested more than $5 billion in the region and paid more than $1.8 billion in federal royalties since its founding. Arena will execute Project Elkhorn alongside affiliated companies White Fleet Drilling and Rosefield Pipeline. The company said the loan closed following technical, legal, environmental and financial due diligence. Additional financial terms were not disclosed. The investment highlights a growing focus on extending production from mature offshore fields, where existing platforms, pipelines and processing facilities can be refurbished to support additional drilling and production without requiring entirely new offshore developments. November 10, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Kalyakan A tanker carrying the first cargo of Russian diesel for the United States has come to a halt off the US east coast, shipping data showed on Tuesday, with its operator saying its destination had not yet been decided. President Donald Trump last month announced a surprise deal with Moscow to import diesel from Russia to help lower prices at the pumps ahead of this month's US midterm elections. The Malta-flagged tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, LSEG shipping data showed, with an expected delivery date of November 7. But the Greece-based company which manages Agioi Fanendes, Eastmed, said a week later that the vessel was proceeding awaiting orders and that a port of discharge had not yet been nominated or finalised. "Nothing has changed regarding the vessel's destination, she is still awaiting orders," Greece-based vessel manager Eastmed told Reuters on Tuesday. Vessels may change their declared destination or revert to "for orders" status more than once during a voyage when a prospective deal falls through, plans change or the operator does not wish to declare its intended destination. Other tankers carrying Russian diesel which had signalled the US Atlantic Coast as their destination later altered course, shipping data showed. RUSSIAN IMPORTS BANNED IN 2022 Former President Joe Biden had imposed a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Trump in approving the deal last month waived parts of a new US sanctions law on Moscow and said Russia would immediately export 300,000 tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter". New Jersey's Democratic Governor Mikie Sherrill this month warned local port officials and terminal operators against accepting Russian diesel, saying those shipments would break federal law. Sherrill said importing Russian diesel could expose businesses and individuals using New Jersey ports to "harsh" civil and criminal penalties. (Reuters)

November 10, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Zerophoto European nations have taken no concrete steps to strengthen shipping protection in the Red Sea, Italy's defence minister said on Tuesday, adding that governments have failed to respond to his calls to bolster the bloc's naval mission in the area. In September, Guido Crosetto urged the European Union to bolster its Aspides mission, launched in 2024 to protect commercial shipping from attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis that have escalated as part of the Middle East conflict. "I have yet to see anything concrete," Crosetto told Reuters, although he said EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas had "fully understood" the importance of Italy's request. Following Crosetto's appeal, Kallas wrote to the bloc's 27 member states urging them to increase their contributions, saying more than 10 warships would be needed for the mission to be truly effective. "About one third of European operations depend on Italy's contribution. Other countries, far larger than us, contribute much, much less," said Crosetto, a senior member of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government. "If it is right to invest in missions, then it is right that everyone contributes," he added, speaking after an event in Rome. articles.summary: Fifty-one years ago today, the SS Edmund Fitzgerald disappeared beneath the waters of Lake Superior during a powerful November storm, taking all 29 crew members with her in one of...

Join the leading maritime news network The SS Edmund Fitzgerald underway on the Great Lakes. The 729-foot freighter sank in Lake Superior on November 10, 1975, with the loss of all 29 crew members. (Photo: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers) Fifty-one years ago today, the SS Edmund Fitzgerald disappeared beneath the waters of Lake Superior during a powerful November storm, taking all 29 crew members with her in one of the most enduring tragedies in Great Lakes maritime history. The 729-foot freighter sank on November 10, 1975, about 17 miles north-northwest of Whitefish Point, Michigan. No distress call was issued, no survivors were found, and the exact circumstances of her final moments remain a subject of debate more than half a century later. On Tuesday, the Great Lakes Shipwreck Historical Society will mark the 51st anniversary with a private memorial ceremony for surviving family members and others connected to the ship and its crew. The 7 p.m. ceremony at Whitefish Point will be livestreamed. The Edmund Fitzgerald was among the largest and best-known freighters operating on the Great Lakes when she departed Superior, Wisconsin, on November 9, 1975, carrying more than 26,000 long tons of taconite iron ore pellets bound for Detroit. Launched in 1958, the vessel had spent 17 years hauling iron ore across the lakes, serving the steel mills that helped power America’s industrial economy. At 729 feet, she was the largest vessel on the Great Lakes when she entered service. On her final voyage, the Fitzgerald , commanded by Capt. Ernest M. McSorley, was accompanied across Lake Superior by the freighter Arthur M. Anderson . As a powerful autumn storm swept across the lake, conditions deteriorated. According to the National Weather Service , winds reached 50 knots, with waves approaching 20 feet. By the afternoon of November 10, the Fitzgerald had reported damage and was taking on water, though the crew did not indicate that the vessel was in immediate danger. The Anderson , following behind, maintained radio contact as the ships made their way toward the shelter of Whitefish Bay. Shortly after 7:10 p.m., the Fitzgerald disappeared from radar. She had gone down without issuing a distress call. The loss prompted an extensive search, but none of the 29 men aboard survived. The cause of the sinking has never been established beyond dispute. A U.S. Coast Guard investigation concluded that the most probable cause was flooding of the cargo hold through ineffective hatch closures. Other theories have focused on structural failure, grounding and the effects of exceptionally large waves. The tragedy also prompted closer scrutiny of Great Lakes vessel safety, including hatch-cover integrity, loading practices and storm-weather operations. The wreck lies in Canadian waters, where it remains a protected gravesite. In 1995, an expedition recovered the ship’s 200-pound bronze bell, which is now displayed at the Great Lakes Shipwreck Museum at Whitefish Point as a permanent memorial to the crew. The disaster became part of American and Canadian popular culture through Gordon Lightfoot’s 1976 ballad, The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald , which introduced generations of listeners to the story of the ship and the men who died aboard her. Lightfoot died in 2023, but his song remains closely associated with the annual remembrance. This year’s commemorations will also include a ceremony at Split Rock Lighthouse in Minnesota, where the names of all 29 crew members will be read aloud to the tolling of a ship’s bell before the lighthouse beacon is illuminated in their honor. For the maritime community, the anniversary is also a reminder of the hazards faced by crews navigating the Great Lakes, particularly during the powerful storms of late autumn. More than five decades after the sinking, the Edmund Fitzgerald remains the largest vessel ever lost on the Great Lakes. And each November 10, the story returns to the 29 mariners who never made it home.
