articles.title: AI at Sea: From Connecting Vessels to Measurable Value
articles.summary: When artificial intelligence (AI) and digitalization are discussed in maritime, attention still gravitates toward autonomous ships. Yet the market is not about de-crewing but, rather, applying vessel and shore data to make operations safer, more fuel-efficient…
articles.body: AI at Sea: From Connecting Vessels to Measurable Value Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Alisa Reiner , Contributor Alisa Reiner is an independent contributor. Alisa brings experience in both... November 10, 2026 Copyright MarineLink.com | Photo by Greg Trauthwein modified with ChatGPT When artificial intelligence (AI) and digitalization are discussed in maritime, attention still gravitates toward autonomous ships. Yet the market is not about de-crewing but, rather, applying vessel and shore data to make operations safer, more fuel-efficient, and easier to maintain. As of 2024, the maritime AI market stood at $4.13 billion, with a projected five-year CAGR of 23%. Market-size estimates should be treated cautiously, but the direction is hard to miss – AI solutions have advanced from trials into voyage planning, machinery monitoring, bridge decision support, port coordination, and digital assurance. The main questions are where it is producing measurable operational value and where the evidence still lags the marketing. The Vessel Has to Be Connected First AI does not create useful ship data – it consumes it. The connected vessel is thus a prerequisite for the AI-capable vessel. Propulsion load, fuel flow, vibration, temperature, pressure, weather, satellite, radar, and camera data are collected through the Internet of Things (IoT) sensors and existing shipboard systems, aggregated and pre-processed onboard, and transmitted to shore via secure communications links. Data quality and context set the ceiling on model performance. Sensor drift, missing values, inconsistent naming, and different operating profiles can affect the lab-tested solution reliability. Latency is another factor – any critical computer vision or machinery control cannot rely on continuous cloud connectivity, so the processing must happen on board. AI and digitalization should not be confused with automation in general. Maritime systems are usually a combination of physics-based models, optimization, rules, and machine learning, not a black-box approach. And sensors, inspection, and edge computing are as important as modeling. Leading companies focus on high-value and repeated use cases, hardware-software-AI integration, and actual customer data. AI and digital tools also serve buyers differently. Table 1 maps key needs to the technologies most directly associated with them, distinguishing shipbuilders’ priorities from those of ship operators. Table 1. What shipowners and shipbuilders want from AI, digitalization, and enabling tools Source: author's analysis Where the Numbers Are Already Visible One of the clearest commercial applications is voyage optimization because fuel consumption provides an immediate KPI. In February 2026, NAPA Voyage Optimization trials demonstrated fuel savings of up to 7.1% on both long and shorter voyages. On the separate 34-day Lila Global voyage from Suez to China, NAPA reported $40,200 in voyage cost savings, 35 tons of fuel saved, 106.5 tons of CO2 avoided, and almost one day less steaming time compared to the simulated standard route. These case studies illustrate why voyage optimization is being scaled – even low-single-digit percentages matter at the fleet level. Computer vision on the bridge is also moving beyond pilots. A 2026 Orca AI study covered 139 vessels and more than 10.8 million nautical miles. High-severity close encounters fell 52% between the early adaptation period and months 10-12. Lloyd's Register separately tested Orca AI on an 828-nautical-mile Mediterranean voyage — across 739 targets, the system achieved 94% precision and 98.6% recall, including small and low-radar-signature craft, with no system downtime. It does not mean that AI should substitute the officer on watch, but machine vision can provide an additional layer of attention when humans, radar, and Automatic Identification System (AIS) face certain limitations. Maintenance presents another application with a measurable business case. Wärtsilä reports that AI-enabled diagnostics reduced unscheduled maintenance by 25% on average, 90% of issues were resolved remotely, and 80% within 24 hours. The operating model here matters – AI detects weak signals and anomalies while engineers validate the diagnosis and reaction. The product thus is not a single algorithm but a combination of sensors, analytics, and expertise. Physical AI is also entering inspection and sustainment. Wall-climbing robots of Gecko Robotics are equipped with ultrasonic sensors to inspect the steel structure of vessels and collect data on its thickness and defects related to corrosion and degradation. In a U.S. Navy application, the system collected more than 4.2 million data points versus around 100 using traditional inspection methods, while a ship-rudder inspection fell from 11 days to one. The data feed digital condition models for maintenance planning and drydock decisions. This example shows another domain where physical AI produces value – by combining robotics with AI-driven analysis of data. Beyond the Ship Ports are another natural target due to the abundance of data on arrival times, berth availability, traffic, weather, and terminal capacity. A 2026 peer-reviewed study of an AI-enabled Just-In-Time (JIT) arrival system reported simulated fuel and emissions savings of 6.45%-7.39% where earlier coordination allowed ships to slow down. Digital twins and data-driven health management are in a similar space – they compare actual behavior of machinery to the expected one to detect deterioration prior to failure. In May 2026, Lloyd's Register granted Approval in Principle to Navantia's AI-based Digital Twin Ready framework. In September 2026, LR also awarded AiP to HD KSOE's VesselWise autonomous auxiliary-machinery optimization function, with onboard validation planned on a 174,000-cbm LNG carrier. AI in maritime is moving from monitoring towards machinery optimization, but the assurance follows closely. Generative AI is less mature operationally. It can make manuals, maintenance histories, and fleet data more searchable or assist shore teams with anomalies investigation. But for now, hard maritime KPI evidence is still scarce in this field, and errors in safety-critical workflows can be costly. Taken together, these examples illustrate the variety of maritime AI applications and their different levels of maturity and autonomy. Figure 1. Maritime AI and digital tools applications: commercial maturity vs degree of autonomous action. Source: author's analytical assessment based on public deployment. Scores are comparative, The Hype Gap Is Mostly a Systems Problem One of the major obstacles to using AI in maritime is not access to a model but integration. AI works in a closed loop – sensors generate data, the model discovers/predicts something valuable, someone makes the decision or controls systems according to the results, and outcomes become feedback. Any disconnected data or process break this loop. The importance of cybersecurity grows as the loop closes. The connected maintenance platform is different from a spreadsheet, and AI integrated with navigation or machinery affects physical operations. IMO has repeatedly highlighted cyber risk across shipboard IT and operational technology. Sensor spoofing, corrupted data, compromised communications, and unauthorized access are therefore not separate IT issues – they are operational risks. Human factors matter too. Too many alerts create alarm fatigue, unexplained recommendations may be ignored, and models can fail in unusual conditions. Crew training, interface design, decision responsibility, and fallback procedures are no less important than model accuracy. From Fancy Tools to Operating System Commercial applications include voyage and speed optimization, computer-vision watchkeeping, condition-based maintenance, and fleet analytics. They solve repetitive, data-rich problems measurable with KPIs on fuel, safety, or downtime. The second group requires proving at scale – autonomous machinery control, AI-enabled digital twins, robotic inspection, generative copilots and highly autonomous ships. With AI moving closer to physical control, validation, cybersecurity, and class approval become more important. For shipowners, the relevant question is not “Do we have AI?” but the decision affected, the data backing it, result measurement, and actions in case of error or offline mode. The winning applications would be those that make a few expensive decisions better. Ultimately, digital tools and AI can help with detection and analysis, but human expertise would still be needed to interpret outputs, take decisions, and apply insights in practice. ▪ Sources 1. Given the scale and complexity of these operations, every decision affects thousands of containers...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Gregor Fischer Hapag-Lloyd, the world’s fifth-largest container carrier, operates 300 vessels on 133 liner services, transporting 13.5 million twenty-foot-equivalent units a year between 600 ports worldwide. Given the scale and complexity of these operations, every decision affects thousands of containers per vessel – with the consequences of any misstep felt throughout the supply chain. The company’s proactive approach to fleetwide digitalisation has therefore been devised with one overarching objective in mind: to simplify its operations. According to Patrick Briest, Hapag-Lloyd’s Senior Director of Operations and IT Products,digitalisation “can do many things”, but making things simpler – from both a commercial and operational perspective – is its one “superpower”. Digitalisation and the connectivity that supports it are increasingly judged by concrete commercial and operational outcomes. “We don’t digitalise just because we can,” Briest told the audience at a recent Inmarsat ‘Connected to Perform’ seminar during SMM 2026. “We digitalise because there’s a use case for it – because there’s value we can drive.” For Hapag-Lloyd, tangible targets include maintaining schedule reliability above 90% across its network, reducing emissions per TEU by 30% by 2030, and approaching net-zero emissions by 2045 – all while cutting operating costs by approximately $100 per TEU. Achieving these goals will require tapping into the “superpower” of digitalisation to facilitate faster and better-informed decisions, said Briest: “We want to enable ourselves, our people, to decide faster, decide better – because we’ve got the data and the tools to understand the impact of every one of the little operational decisions we make all the time.” To illustrate the benefits of digitalisation and connectivity on Hapag-Lloyd’s operations, Briest presented a notional voyage involving a container ship transporting perishable goods from the west coast of South America to Northern Europe. If a crane were to fail during the vessel’s final port call in South America, he said, the consequentdelays might result in the ship missing its slot to cross the Panama Canal. However, by retrieving operational data from the vessel’s digital cargo logbook, Hapag-Lloyd would know by exactly how long to extend its port call to maximise cargo intake without sacrificing its slot. Later, if the vessel were to encounter extreme weather in the Atlantic Ocean, the operator would combine specific vessel data points with shore-based analysis to evaluate routing, speed, fuel consumption, and port arrival options. In this way, Briest explained, Hapag-Lloyd could keep commercial and environmental impacts to a minimum without compromising voyage safety. Digitalisation and connectivity, then, enable shipping companies like Hapag-Lloyd to make smarter operational decisions based on a richer and more immediate view of what is happening on the vessel and across the network. As Briest demonstrated in the second scenario, they also help close the gap between ship and shore. In another example, IT support teams can now connect directly with the vessel, remotely accessing even the engine room to help resolve technical issues efficiently. Whereas ships previously operated as isolated assets, they increasingly function as an extension of head office, with seafarers and shorestaff working as one team, and the Atlantic Ocean – in Briest’s words – becoming “as connected as downtown Frankfurt”. Digitalisation is connecting vessels not only to their operator’s headquarters but also with the clientswhose goods they transport. In a further operational scenario from the notional voyage, Briest explained that the Hapag-Lloyd LIVE tool allows customers to monitor refrigerated cargo and respond when circumstances change. If the vessel is delayed, temperature settings can be adjusted remotely to help ensure the cargo reaches its destination in optimal condition. “By being more digital, we want to be as easy to do business with for our customers as we possibly can be,” he commented. Recognising that increased connectivity also has its challenges, Hapag-Lloyd’s digitalisation strategy emphasises cybersecurity and seafarer autonomy to maintain operational resilience. “As we connect more systems on the vessel, we’re of course creating a substantially bigger attack surface,” Briest acknowledged, adding that the company is “pushing between 100 and 200 patches to every vessel every week” to address this issue. Cybersecurity, he said, “cannot be an afterthought anymore” – instead, it should be “secure by design and [built] from the ground up”. At the same time, Hapag-Lloyd is taking care to ensure digitalisation strengthens rather than weakens the judgement, resilience, and practical competency of its seafarers. “Digitalisation can help a lot, but there’s an inherent [seafaring] culture, capability and skillset that we also need to preserve,” said Briest. These considerations become increasingly important as Hapag-Lloyd’s digitalisation strategy progresses. As more decisions, systems, applications, and interactions come to depend on the ship–shore connection, and the vessel is further integrated into the broader digital operating environment, connectivity itself becomes strategic infrastructure. Inmarsat Maritime’s NexusWave is a key enabler of Hapag-Lloyd’s digitalisation strategy. The fully managed, bonded multi-network connectivity solution delivers the consistent high speeds, global reliability, and secure-by-design infrastructure the company needs to continue its transformation and pursue its operational ambitions with confidence. Digitalisation, Briest summarised, is helping Hapag-Lloyd to manage its workload, make better decisions, and work more effectively as a team – both onboard the vessel and between ship and shore. While he stressed that connectivity needs to be managed responsibly to preserve cybersecurity and crew autonomy, he was in no doubt about the direction of travel: “The future of shipping is connected,” he concluded. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo A vessel operated by ADNOC Logistics & Services was damaged in an attack in UAE territorial waters on Tuesday, as maritime authorities reported a separate apparent projectile strike against a tanker near the Strait of Hormuz, adding to a growing series of attacks on commercial shipping in the region. ADNOC Logistics & Services confirmed that one of its vessels sustained damage in an attack in the Persian Gulf on the afternoon of November 10. In a statement carried by the UAE’s state-run WAM news agency, the company said response operations were ongoing but provided no details about the vessel’s identity, the extent of the damage or whether any crew members were injured. The company said further updates would be provided as information became available. The announcement came as the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that a tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile approximately 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman, near the strategically important Strait of Hormuz. According to UKMTO Warning 201-26 , the incident occurred at 1338 UTC on November 10. The vessel’s master reported that all crew members were safe and there was no environmental impact. A damage assessment was planned for first light. UKMTO did not identify the tanker or establish the origin of the projectile. It was not immediately clear whether the ADNOC incident and the strike reported by UKMTO were connected or represented separate attacks. The latest developments follow a series of incidents along the Omani side of the Strait of Hormuz, where vessels have faced projectile strikes, fires and other hostile activity in recent days. On November 7, a tanker caught fire approximately eight nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, forcing its crew to evacuate. UKMTO initially reported the incident based on information from military authorities before subsequently reclassifying it as an attack . Another tanker transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz was reportedly struck by an unidentified projectile on November 7. Its crew was reported safe, with no environmental impact. The incidents come as maritime security authorities continue to warn of an exceptionally dangerous operating environment in and around the strait. In its November 8 advisory , the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) maintained the threat level for the Strait of Hormuz at SEVERE, warning that further deliberate attacks were highly likely. JMIC reported five attacks off Oman’s Musandam coast between November 1 and November 5, followed by additional incidents on November 7. The center said 177 maritime security incidents had been recorded across the wider region since March 1. That figure includes suspicious activity and military enforcement incidents, rather than attacks against merchant vessels alone. Commercial traffic through the waterway remains far below normal levels. According to JMIC, independent tracking indicated daily transits in the single digits to low double digits, compared with a historical average of approximately 138 vessels per day in 2025. U.S. naval shipping coordination figures, meanwhile, indicated 91 U.S.-facilitated transits between November 5 and 7, averaging roughly 30 per day. The figures reflect different reporting systems and vessel populations and are not directly comparable. The disruption has left large numbers of vessels waiting outside the waterway. JMIC estimated that approximately 162 ships were anchored near Fujairah and Khor Fakkan as of November 8, with additional concentrations near Sohar and Musandam. The center warned that continued attacks, Iranian monitoring of commercial shipping and U.S. naval blockade enforcement were likely to keep shipping operators cautious and traffic depressed. Tuesday’s reported attacks add to mounting concerns over the safety of merchant vessels and their crews in one of the world’s most important energy shipping corridors, where repeated security incidents continue to complicate commercial transit despite efforts to facilitate vessel movements. The historic SS United States will be sunk off Florida’s Gulf Coast a day earlier than planned after forecasts of heavy winds forced officials to move up the operation. Okaloosa County announced Monday that the 990-foot ocean liner will be deployed as the world’s largest artificial reef on Wednesday, November 11, instead of Thursday, November 12. Deployment operations are now scheduled to begin at 1 p.m. Central Standard Time. The change comes as the legendary ocean liner makes its final voyage from Mobile, Alabama , to a designated reef site approximately 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach. “Safety is always a top priority in Okaloosa County,” said County Board Chairman Trey Goodwin. “There is simply no reason to take an unnecessary risk when adjusting the schedule will allow us to carry out this historic deployment safely and smoothly.” The schedule change also means the public sendoff ceremony originally planned for Wednesday afternoon at the Destin-Fort Walton Beach Convention Center has been canceled. However, a public viewing party will still take place at AJ’s Seafood and Oyster Bar in Destin beginning at noon Wednesday. A live feed of the offshore deployment will be shown on the venue’s large outdoor screen, with an online livestream link expected to be posted at thessus.com before operations begin. County officials are also preparing for potentially hundreds of spectator vessels near the deployment site and are urging boaters to follow instructions from safety boats overseeing the operation. The deployment will take place on Veterans Day, adding another layer of significance to the final chapter of America’s most famous ocean liner. Built in 1952, the SS United States still holds the record for the fastest transatlantic crossing by an ocean liner. Following decades of inactivity, the vessel has undergone extensive environmental remediation in Mobile in preparation for its transformation into an artificial reef. The sinking will mark the end of the ship’s 74-year history above water and the beginning of a new role as a diving destination and marine habitat off Florida’s Emerald Coast. articles.body: Marlink Secures BV Certification for XChange NextGen Platform Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 © Marlink Marlink has secured Bureau Veritas (BV) type approval for the XChange NextGen edge platform, giving shipowners independent assurance that their onboard digital infrastructure is designed with long-term cyber resilience built-in. For shipowners, onboard technology is a long-term investment that can remain in service for years. As software evolves and new services are introduced, cybersecurity must remain a priority throughout the platform’s lifecycle. XChange NextGen’s type approval confirms compliance with requirements covering both cybersecurity capabilities and the processes supporting secure development, maintenance and updates. XChange NextGen is Marlink’s onboard platform, combining edge computing with connectivity, network orchestration, cybersecurity and cloud services to support secure digital operations. Its edge capability allows data to be processed on board, giving shipowners a foundation for analytics and AI applications that depend on reliable data flow between vessel and shore. As part of the Marlink Possibility Portfolio, it reduces hardware complexity and enables vessel and shore teams to deploy, manage and scale digital services more easily across fleets. The certification confirms compliance with IACS UR E27 Rev.1 and Bureau Veritas NR659 requirements within the approved scope. While IACS UR E26 addresses cyber resilience at vessel level, UR E27 focuses on individual onboard systems and equipment, providing shipowners, shipyards and systems integrators with evidence to support applicable class requirements. XChange NextGen’s E27 type approval complements Marlink’s wider approach to vessel cyber resilience. Its OT Security offering helps shipowners identify and manage cyber risks in operational systems, supporting their broader work to meet applicable vessel-level requirements, including IACS UR E26.

articles.title: Cflow Provides Fish Handling System for Brønnbåt Wellboat
articles.summary: Brønnbåt Nord's largest wellboat to date will be equipped with a complete fish handling system from Cflow in Langevåg, on Norway's west coast. The solutions have been further developed to ensure good conditions for the fish, gentler handling…
articles.body: Cflow Provides Fish Handling System for Brønnbåt Wellboat Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 © Cflow Brønnbåt Nord's largest wellboat to date will be equipped with a complete fish handling system from Cflow in Langevåg, on Norway's west coast. The solutions have been further developed to ensure good conditions for the fish, gentler handling and efficient operations on board. With a cargo capacity of 5,000 cubic meters, the new wellboat can carry the equivalent of approximately 4.2 million salmon dinners in a single trip to the processing plant. The investment will help meet growing demand for wellboat capacity in Northern Norway. Brønnbåt Nord is owned by the aquaculture companies Salaks, Gratanglaks and Kleiva Fiskefarm. The vessel has been designed by NSK Ship Design in Harstad and will be built at Zamakona Shipyard in Bilbao, Spain, with delivery scheduled for 2029. The newbuild will feature battery-hybrid propulsion, an energy-efficient hull design and the capacity to produce up to 10,000 cubic meters of freshwater on board. The new vessel will be equipped with several further-developed Cflow solutions designed to ensure good water quality and greater control over the conditions fish are exposed to during transport and handling. Cflow's delivery includes complete systems for fish handling, water circulation and treatment, hygiene, automation and data logging. It also features high-capacity CO2 degassing systems, systems for regulating total gas pressure (TGP), and nanobubble generators from Cflow's partner Moleaer, which supply oxygen to the water. The nanobubble generators inject very small oxygen bubbles that remain in the water for longer, rather than quickly rising to the surface. According to Cflow, this enables more efficient use of oxygen compared with traditional venturi injectors. The vessel will be equipped with fish loading and unloading lines with a diameter of 600 millimeters (DN600), designed to handle high capacities during loading and unloading. This will enable efficient fish handling and shorter operation times, while keeping fish welfare a key priority. Cflow will also deliver piping systems designed for cleaning in place (CIP), without the need for dismantling. This will simplify cleaning procedures and help maintain good hygiene between operations. In addition, the vessel will be equipped with fish counters from Wingtech, adapted for different operations on board. The counters will record the number of fish during loading and unloading, and one of the counters will also be suitable for smolt counting. This will give the shipping company better control over the number of fish being handled. Cflow and Brønnbåt Nord previously collaborated on the battery-hybrid wellboat MS Caspian , delivered in 2024. Experience gained from that project has been carried forward into the development of solutions for the new vessel. Although the vessel will be built in Spain, approximately 40 per cent of the deliveries will come from Norwegian companies. For Cflow, based in Langevåg near Alesund, the contract means significant activity in the years ahead, helping to support local employment and further development of the company's technology expertise.

articles.title: From basic wave data to trusted predictive decision support
articles.summary: What turns a wave measurement into a prediction your crew can trust?
articles.body: Branded Content November 10, 2026 · 41 minutes ago From basic wave data to trusted predictive decision support What turns a wave measurement into a prediction your crew can trust? Written in partnership with Miros 7 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Start with the operational question: Do you understand the wave conditions around your vessel during operations? Can the crew find the measurement when they need it? Can they explain what significant wave height and wave period mean for this vessel and this task? Source: Miros real-time WaveSystem dashboard showcase (AI Illustration) Author: Lars Ivar Leivestad, Commercial Manager at Miros Picture a vessel holding position offshore. The next operation has been carefully planned, the crew is briefed, and the weather forecast suggests conditions are within operational limits. But then the vessel starts moving more than expected. The sea looks much the same as it did earlier. Is this a temporary variation or a sign of changing sea conditions? Will it now impact the lifting operation, personnel transfer or equipment deployment about to begin? How can the crew make an informed decision about whether to proceed? Local, real-time sea state measurements can help. By providing an accurate picture of the sea conditions around the vessel, they help bridge the gap between forecasts and what is happening offshore. But having access to data is only the first step. The real value comes from understanding the measurements, connecting them to operational decisions and building more advanced capabilities as needs evolve. Start with the operational question: Do you understand the wave conditions around your vessel during operations? Begin with a task the crew recognizes. For a Chief Officer preparing a deck cargo transfer on a platform supply vessel, that might mean understanding the wave conditions along the vessel during the operation. Identify the question and the people who need the answer. One of our offshore vessel customers began with just such a need. They already had forecasts and experienced personnel, but wanted a continuous, measured real-time reference for the local sea state. The first installation used a single non-contact wave sensor, with significant wave height and wave period as the initial parameters. Forecasts remain part of planning. Real-time measurements add information about conditions at the measurement location. Before you add more data, decide what the first measurement is for. Name the decision it should inform. For the Chief Officer, that could be the call on whether to start the deck cargo transfer. Then set a first goal the team can check. Can the crew find the measurement when they need it? Can they explain what significant wave height and wave period mean for this vessel and this task? Are they using it in the go/no-go discussions you identified? Once the answer to each is yes, crew and management share a clear baseline. Know what the number represents: Is the sensor wrong, or are you comparing two different things? Say a larger wave passes the vessel while the significant wave height changes little. Significant wave height, commonly written Hs, is a statistical measure approximately corresponding to the average height of the highest third of waves. Individual waves can be higher. Wave period is the time between successive wave crests passing a fixed point. Displays can present it in more than one way, so confirm which period parameter yours shows. The measurement context is equally important. Identify the sensor location, the area or point it observes, the reporting interval and the quality information available. Understand how the system accounts for vessel motion. A downward-looking range measurement from a moving platform needs appropriate motion compensation to distinguish surface movement from sensor movement. A reading from one point on the vessel does not describe every point around the hull. Check the timestamp and the averaging period used for statistical parameters. Those details help distinguish a live display update from the passage of an individual wave. Ask the watch team to explain the parameter in relation to the task. Significant wave height, commonly written Hs, is a statistical measure approximately corresponding to the average height of the highest third of waves. Individual waves can be higher. The measurement context is important. Source: Miros varying sea condition illustration (AI Illustration) Build confidence through operational use: When the sea changes, what changes on the display? Give the team opportunities to compare measurements with conditions and vessel behavior during normal work. When a measurement seems surprising, review the observation, the parameter definition and the data quality together. In our customer’s initial experience, personnel compared wave readings with what they could see and feel. Over time, they began relating combinations of wave height and period to their vessel’s behavior. A Master and Chief Officer can bring that same learning into a briefing: the measured conditions, the planned task and the relevant operating limits. Recording the conditions and the vessel’s operating state gives later reviews something specific to examine. Visual agreement helps build familiarity, but technical verification is still necessary to confirm measurement performance. Confidence requires both reliable measurements and an understanding of their operational significance. Progress shows when people can explain what the readings mean for their work, identify gaps and raise questions that experience alone or the initial parameters do not fully answer. Add context when the question changes: Why can a familiar significant wave height accompany a different vessel response? Wave period and direction relative to heading can help explain the difference. Waves approaching the bow, beam or stern do not produce the same response in every case. Add directional information when it addresses a specific operational need. Surface current measurement can provide further context for a Dynamic Positioning Officer considering environmental conditions on a construction support vessel. It does not provide a current profile through the water column. This expansion requires the right measurement configuration. Combining X-band radar with a downward-looking wave sensor adds directional wave and surface-current information to the local wave measurements. Before interpreting directional data, confirm the reference frame and conventions in the system documentation. Wave direction must be understood in relation to the vessel’s heading and the operation. The key question: Can users understand and explain the purpose of each additional measurement? Confirm the required equipment, interfaces and data quality before introducing new parameters. Video clip: 3D vessel view 3D interface in Miros WaveSystem, showing where each wave measurement is taken. It brings each installed measurement source, its measurement area and the key wave values together in one intuitive display, providing a bird’s-eye view of the sea state data most relevant to safeguard operations. Source: Miros WaveSystem 3D vessel visualization Connect the waves with the vessel: Which approaching waves and associated motions would be useful to anticipate? Now bring measured vessel response into the discussion. Vessel design, size, loading condition, heading and operating mode all influence how a vessel responds to the sea. Wave height alone cannot describe the implications for every operation. For a service operation vessel preparing a gangway connection, relate the environmental conditions to vessel motions and the applicable equipment and operational limits. For a research or survey vessel recovering an instrument, connect the wave conditions with the motions affecting equipment handling. Assess these relationships in the context of the specific vessel and operation. Keep wave measurements, vessel motions and equipment performance distinct. Understanding one does not automatically establish the others. Identify the motion, such as heave, roll or pitch, and where on the vessel it matters. Measure or predict where it matters. Bring measured vessel response into the discussion. Vessel design, size, loading condition, heading and operating mode all influence how a vessel responds to the sea. Wave height alone cannot describe the implications for every operation. Source: Cable lay vessel, Adobe Stock Evaluate the prediction against actual outcomes: How do you know the prediction is right? Approach prediction with the same discipline as the initial measurements. Establish what is being predicted, how far ahead, under which conditions and with what level of uncertainty. Miros’ PredictifAI technology, for example, combines X-band radar observations of incoming waves, local downward-looking wave measurements and artificial intelligence. It provides deterministic predictions of waves and vessel motion, including when they will occur. The published prediction horizon ranges from seconds to a couple of minutes, depending on installation and operating conditions. Available predicted output depends on the installation. Motions influenced by dynamic positioning, navigation or crane operations cannot automatically be predicted from wave measurements alone. Compare predictions with subsequent measurements to assess their accuracy. Consider the timing and size of the event, the uncertainty involved and the conditions in which the comparison was made. Review the results with relevant personnel before deciding how predictions should support operations. The available prediction might support a critical phase of a lifting operation or a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) deployment. But the prediction horizon alone cannot establish suitability for an entire operation extending beyond it. Understanding the measurements helps users look beyond the “black box.” Confidence starts with reliable input data, but predictions must also demonstrate their accuracy and operational value. It provides deterministic wave and vessel motion prediction, from seconds to a couple of minutes, depending on installation and operating conditions. Source: Miros PredictifAI traffic light display Make the information part of the watch The next watch should also be able to use and question the information. Integrate it into training, handovers, toolbox talks and operational reviews, ensuring its role within existing procedures is clear. Establish how personnel should respond when data is unavailable or unreliable. A Marine Operations Manager with access to the same measurements can discuss plans with the offshore team using a shared understanding of conditions. A Marine Superintendent can help integrate the technology into training and procedures, in line with the operator’s defined responsibilities. A Coast Guard vessel preparing to launch or recover a small boat must also consider local sea conditions and vessel motions in the context of the task. Prediction remains one input alongside forecasts, procedures, measured conditions and established operational limits. Qualified personnel retain responsibility for operational decisions. Back on board, the next operation still requires a decision. Better-informed discussions can start with a single trusted measurement, then build toward directional waves, surface currents, vessel response and prediction. Measure. Understand. Trust. Expand. Predict. One trusted measurement. One practical step at a time. Some organizations may benefit from a more comprehensive system from the outset. For those new to wave monitoring, the priority is to establish the value of the initial measurements before expanding. Which operational question could your team answer more confidently with access to accurate, local, real-time sea state measurements? articles.body: Exploration & Production November 10, 2026 · 13 minutes ago First oil from Southeast Asian offshore project flows sooner than expected The start of production from an offshore platform at an oil field in Vietnamese waters comes 36 days ahead of schedule. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Oil production has kicked off from BK-26 platform at Bach Ho field Source: Vietsovpetro Beating its planned start date by more than a month, the Vietnam-Russia joint venture Vietsovpetro has achieved its first oil flow from a wellhead platform at the Bach Ho field off the coast of Vietnam to boost its 2026 output amid natural field declines and strengthen the Southeast Asian country's energy security. The first oil milestone that was recorded on November 9, 2026, has enabled Vietsovpetro to bring online the BK-26 platform at the Bach Ho field in Block 09-1 offshore Vietnam. The beginning of production was achieved 36 days ahead of the approved timeline set by the Intergovernmental Council, because it was originally scheduled for December 15, 2026. The early start-up is interpreted to directly augment domestic crude oil output, strongly supporting the fulfillment of Vietsovpetro and Petrovietnam’s 2026 production and business targets. The project enables field optimization by securing stable, sustainable reservoir extraction and extending the economic life of the offshore Bach Ho field in the coming years. Petrovietnam emphasized: “This achievement highlights Vietsovpetro’s proven project execution capabilities, engineering excellence, and the enduring effectiveness of Vietnam - Russia energy cooperation. "By continuously optimizing offshore infrastructure, Petrovietnam firmly reinforces its mission of safeguarding national energy security.” On November 3, the Vietsovpetro Acceptance Council conducted the overall acceptance of the BK-26 project, issued a decision to put it into use on November 5, and assessed the completion level of the project to ensure operational safety. Since the output at Vietsovpetro's traditional oil fields is in a process of natural decline, Petrovietnam highlights that putting BK-26 into operation ahead of schedule is of great significance. Petrovietnam noted: “The oil flow from BK26 not only marks the introduction of a new project into operation but is also the result of the synchronous coordination process between units participating in the project. “Ensuring progress in offshore construction conditions facing many weather disadvantages, continuing to affirm the ability to master from exploration, design, construction to management, operation and exploitation of offshore oil and gas projects; and at the same time showing the spirit of responsibility and high determination of Vietsovpetro's collective of workers.” Related Articles Fossil Energy Petrovietnam and Gazprom outline drilling plans to boost gas production off Vietnam 2 min read The BK-26 project entails the BK-26 wellhead platform and bridge connecting to MSP-8; MSP-8 renovation to receive and process products from BK-26; and relocation of MSP8-MSP4 underground power cable line. articles.title: Ofgem names preferred bidder for Dogger Bank B offshore transmission assets
articles.summary: A consortium of Diamond Transmission UK (DTUK) and Japan’s Chubu Electric Power has been selected as the preferred bidder to acquire and operate...
articles.body: News November 10, 2026 · 1 minute ago Ofgem names preferred bidder for Dogger Bank B offshore transmission assets AB Adrijana Buljan Offshore Wind 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Dogger Bank Wind Farm A consortium of Diamond Transmission UK (DTUK) and Japan’s Chubu Electric Power has been selected as the preferred bidder to acquire and operate the offshore transmission assets connecting the 1.2 GW Dogger Bank B wind farm to the UK grid. The transmission system, valued at approximately £1 billion (around €1.2 billion) by the consortium, comprises subsea and onshore cables, an offshore converter station and an onshore converter station. The consortium will operate the transmission business for 25 years after acquiring the assets and receiving an Offshore Transmission Owner (OFTO) licence from the UK energy regulator. The preferred bidder appointment is part of Ofgem’s Tender Round 11 process. Ofgem launched the tender round in February 2024 and shortlisted four bidder groups in July that year. Ofgem appointed the consortium of DTUK and Chubu as the preferred bidder on November 5. Dogger Bank B, located approximately 130 kilometers off the UK’s east coast, is the second phase of the world’s largest offshore wind farm under construction, the 3.6 GW Dogger Bank Wind Farm, owned by the consortium of SSE Renewables, Equinor, and Vårgrønn. The second phase is currently under construction, with wind turbine installation underway . The Dogger Bank B transmission system uses high-voltage direct current (HVDC) technology to transmit electricity from the offshore wind farm to the National Grid. Its offshore converter station was installed in April 2024 by Saipem’s Saipem 7000 heavy-lift vessel. DTUK is wholly owned by Global Infrastructure Partners, part of BlackRock. Following the acquisition, the company will operate eleven UK OFTO projects with a combined capacity of almost 7 GW and a total transferred asset value exceeding GBP 5.5 billion (around €6.6 billion), according to the consortium. For Chubu, the Dogger Bank B project will be its third UK offshore transmission investment, following its participation alongside DTUK in the Walney Extension and Hornsea 1 OFTO projects. The Japanese utility said it would contribute its technical expertise in transmission systems while building experience in HVDC technology and the operation and maintenance of subsea transmission assets. articles.title: Seabed monitoring starts at UK CCS project to prepare for CO2 injection
articles.summary: Six lander systems have been installed at the Northern Endurance Partnership (NEP) project, the UK's first commercial-scale offshore carbon...
articles.body: Carbon Capture Usage & Storage November 10, 2026 · 1 hour ago Seabed monitoring starts at UK CCS project to prepare for CO2 injection NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Sonardyne Six lander systems have been installed at the Northern Endurance Partnership (NEP) project, the UK's first commercial-scale offshore carbon capture and storage (CCS) project, to monitor the seabed before CO2 injection starts. Sonardyne, a Kraken Robotics company, reported the start of baseline environmental and passive seismic monitoring at the project, following the deployment of the six seabed lander systems at the Endurance CO2 store, in the Southern North Sea, about 150 kilometers off the coast of Teesside. The monitoring landers will support the long-term measurement, monitoring and verification (MMV) program for offshore CO2 storage by helping establish the robust, repeatable data needed to monitor the reservoir integrity effectively over time. Three autonomous environmental monitoring landers designed and built by Sonardyne and three co-located TIAMAT passive seismic monitoring systems from K.U.M. are collecting baseline data on seawater chemistry, currents, seabed conditions and passive seismic activity before future CO2 injection operations begin. This will support continued monitoring across the storage lifecycle. “Confidence in offshore CO₂ storage starts with good data. By delivering and deploying these environmental and micro-seismic monitoring systems, and managing their ongoing operation and data retrieval, Sonardyne is supporting a key part of NEP’s MMV programme at Endurance," said Stephen Auld , Business Development Manager for Custom Projects at Sonardyne. “For offshore CO₂ storage, that continuity matters. Long-term assurance depends on reliable data gathered across the full storage lifecycle, not a single point-in-time measurement — a role that draws directly on our experience in seabed-resident monitoring, acoustic communications and offshore integrity monitoring.” NEP, a joint venture of BP, Equinor and TotalEnergies, is delivering CO2 transportation and storage infrastructure centred on the Endurance store, which is about 1,000 meters beneath the seabed, as part of the East Coast Cluster decarbonization program across Teesside and the Humber. Storage is expected to start in 2028, making it the first operational CCS project in the UK. The initial phase is expected to see up to 100 million tons of CO2 stored in the Endurance aquifer over a 25-year period. “The deployment of these monitoring systems is a great example of the expertise and innovation that is helping to deliver CCS in the UK. Establishing a robust environmental and seismic baseline before operations begin, is a vital part of our long-term monitoring programme, providing the data required to demonstrate the safe and secure storage of CO₂ over time," said Mike Stephen , Head of Technical at NEP.
